newsitem.title: CHINA: China warns Japan to learn from aggressive past.
newsitem.headline: China warns Japan to learn from aggressive past.

text.p: China's President Jiang Zemin has urged Japan not to forget its invasion of China 60 years ago, saying history served as a lesson for the future, the People's Daily said on Thursday.
However, Jiang told visiting former Japanese prime minister Tsutomu Hata in a meeting on Wednesday that ties had expanded significantly since they were established a quarter of a century ago.
"The two sides should pay twice as much attention to the hard-won friendly relationship and cherish it," Jiang was quoted as saying.
But he warned Japan not to forget its history of atrocities in China and the launch 60 years ago of Tokyo's full-scale invasion of China in which Beijing says 35 million Chinese were casualties.
"The unforgotten past will be a lesson for the future," Jiang told his Japanese visitor.
"Japan can hold the future in its hand and pursue a route of peaceful development only if it can correctly recall its role in history," Jiang was quoted as saying.

Beijing regularly reminds Japan that it must not forget its aggression in China and Asia and has issued several tirades against Japanese militarism in recent days to mark the July 7 anniversary of the start of Tokyo's invasion 60 years ago.
Analysts say China is also almost certain to use the 25th anniversary this year of the establishment of formal ties to focus on its often troubled relations with Japan.
Jiang urged leaders and statesmen of both countries to adopt a strategic perspective and to handle relations to ensure their healthy and steady development.

The People's Daily, mouthpiece of the ruling Communist Party, issued a stinging editorial warning of a rising tide of militarism among extremists in Japan and urged Tokyo's leaders not to ignore the resurgence.
"Some frantic militarist trumpeters in present Japan are trying to justify the crimes and atrocities," the editorial said. "What a logic of bandits."
It reminded Tokyo that diplomatic ties were set up 25 years ago only after Japan accepted responsibility for the war.
"In the 25 years thereafter, Japanese leaders in general have shown a gradual progress toward a better understanding on this point," it said.
However, Japanese militarists today were reviving the "national spirit" of the 1930s, it railed, and warned against their future influence.
"Where on earth are they going to lead Japan to? What international image are they going to help make for Japan?" the editorial said.
"Sensible statesmen and people of insight in Japan should not keep their eyes closed and let their country be led astray by these people," it said.

"The Chinese people hope that Japan will choose the road of peaceful development and carry the Sino-Japanese friendship from generation to generation," it said. "And a start point of the road is to have a correct attitude toward history."
